extracted.intended_audience: Recipients of Federal financial assistance (educational institutions), Title IX Coordinators, campus administrators, and legal/compliance staff implementing Title IX grievance and informal resolution procedures
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory requirements for establishing and operating Title IX informal resolution processes and grievance procedures (including postsecondary-specific rules) to resolve complaints of sex discrimination. Covers notice requirements, facilitator training and impartiality, permissible terms of informal resolution agreements, privacy protections, due process principles, and postsecondary procedural safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of potential terms in informal resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: The recipient must provide notice of the potential terms that may be requested or offered in an informal resolution agreement, including notice that an informal resolution agreement is binding only on the parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revised §106.44(k)(3)(v) requires recipients to give parties the general framework and parameters of possible resolution terms so parties can provide informed consent; the notice need not list every possible measure, remedy, or sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of what information will be maintained and disclosed
rubrics_metrics.description: The recipient must explain to the parties what information related to informal resolution it may maintain and whether and how it could disclose such information if grievance procedures are initiated or resumed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revised §106.44(k)(3)(vi) balances informing parties of consequences of pursuing informal resolution with allowing recipients flexibility to structure processes appropriate to their programs; the notice should make clear what may or may not be disclosed for use in §106.45 (and, if applicable, §106.46) grievance procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal resolution facilitator training and impartiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person facilitating informal resolution must receive appropriate training and must not have a conflict of interest or bias for or against complainants or respondents generally or an individual complainant or respondent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §106.44(k)(4) requires facilitators to be trained under §106.8(d)(3). The Department declined to permit facilitators to serve as investigators because doing so risks the appearance of bias that could erode trust and impair fair outcomes; use of outside entities may alleviate concerns in single-investigator models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy protections during informal resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient must comply with §106.44(j) when conducting informal resolution and must not disclose personally identifiable information about participants except in the circumstances enumerated in that provision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informal resolution notice requirements should inform parties of privacy limits; recipients must be careful about maintaining or disclosing information and must explain such limits under §106.44(k)(3)(vi).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible terms of informal resolution agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may agree to informal resolution terms that the recipient could have imposed at the conclusion of its grievance procedures, including restrictions on contact and restrictions on participation in programs or activities that the recipient could have imposed as remedies or disciplinary sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §106.44(k)(5)(ii) makes clear that illustrative lists in §106.44(k)(5) are non-exhaustive (‘include but are not limited to’). Restrictions on contact may be mutual or non‑mutual; recipients may impose restrictions as supportive measures during grievance proceedings or as terms of an informal resolution agreement. Recipients should ensure parties understand potential consequences (e.g., no-contact orders) and parental/legal representative rights under §106.6.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties' right to decline or withdraw from informal resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties have the right to decline an offer to participate in, or withdraw from, a recipient's informal resolution process prior to agreeing to a resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent with §106.44(k)(2) and (3)(iii), notices must inform parties of this right so they can make informed choices; recipients should ensure parties understand alternatives (i.e., pursuing formal grievance procedures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient discretion to choose appropriate informal resolution methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Informal resolution may encompass a wide variety of alternative dispute resolution processes (mediation, restorative justice, transformative justice, etc.), and the recipient has discretion to choose options best suited for the parties and educational community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department recognizes concerns that mediation may be inappropriate for allegations like sexual assault (risk of retraumatization, pressure on complainant). Nothing in the final regulations precludes restorative or transformative justice practices; recipients should assess appropriateness case-by-case and may decline mediation when inappropriate. The Department will provide technical assistance as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grievance procedures must be prompt and equitable
rubrics_metrics.description: Final §106.45 requires grievance procedures that provide for the prompt and equitable resolution of complaints of sex discrimination generally and sets basic elements of a fair process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §106.45 applies to a wide range of recipients (elementary, secondary, postsecondary, state agencies, libraries, museums, etc.) and is intended to ensure transparency, equity, trauma-informed care, and reliable outcomes while allowing recipient flexibility to tailor procedures to their environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postsecondary-specific procedural protections (§106.46)
rubrics_metrics.description: For sex-based harassment involving a student party at a postsecondary institution, §106.46 incorporates additional procedural requirements appropriate to the age, maturity, independence, needs, and context of students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retained provisions include: opportunity to have an advisor of the party's choice at any meeting or proceeding (§106.46(e)(2)); allowing a party's advisor to ask relevant (and not otherwise impermissible) questions during a live hearing (§106.46(f)(1)(ii)(B)); and opportunity to appeal based on procedural irregularity, new evidence, conflict of interest or bias, and any other equally-offered bases (§106.46(i)(1)-(2)). These measures ensure adequate notice, access to evidence, and appeal rights in the postsecondary context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice and access to evidence; address false statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must provide adequate written notice of allegations and ensure parties have access to relevant and not otherwise impermissible evidence; recipients retain authority to prohibit parties and witnesses from knowingly making false statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisions cited (§106.46(c), (d), (e)(1), (e)(5), (c)(1)(iv)) require written notice of allegations, dismissal, meetings, interviews, hearings, and delays; equal opportunity to access relevant evidence; and written notice informing parties of any code-of-conduct provisions prohibiting knowingly making false statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process protections must be preserved and context-sensitive
rubrics_metrics.description: Grievance procedures must comport with due process while affording recipients flexibility to tailor procedures to their educational environment; what process is due varies with circumstances and is informed by constitutional and Supreme Court precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department affirms that procedural due process is important but not monolithic—courts recognize variation (e.g., Mathews v. Eldridge balancing, Goss v. Lopez standards for student suspension). Final rules do not impose different standards for public vs. private recipients beyond constitutional limits and do not permit the Department to require recipients to deny constitutional rights (34 CFR 106.6(d)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for determining what process is due
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients should determine what process is due based on the nature of the proceedings and relevant legal tests rather than by mechanically adopting criminal or civil judicial procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters referenced Mathews v. Eldridge; the Department reiterates that procedures must be fair but not identical to judicial proceedings. Minimum due process generally includes timely notice of charges and an opportunity for the respondent to review evidence and present their side, but specifics should be calibrated to context (e.g., age, severity, potential sanctions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory stability and flexibility to tailor procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations retain and enhance aspects of the 2020 amendments while restoring certain longstanding interpretations to provide stability; recipients are afforded flexibility to design Title IX grievance procedures consistent with due process and their institutional context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The framework aims to promote regulatory stability to facilitate broad understanding and compliance, while allowing recipients to account for structural differences (population size, staffing, resources) and to adopt models (e.g., single-investigator) within the guardrails of the final regulations.
